newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany in deal on 800 mln DM Soviet debt payback.
newsitem.headline: Germany in deal on 800 mln DM Soviet debt payback.

text.p: German business groups said on Friday they had agreed with Russia's finance ministry to convert delinquent Soviet trade debts, not covered by state guarantees, into long-term bonds.

The Federation of German Industry (BDI) said in a statement that, under a framework deal, 800 million marks owed since the early 1990s to German firms would be switched into promissory notes of the old Soviet foreign trade bank Vneshekonombank.

The agreement, reached in London after three years of talks, is part of a multilateral deal reached by 12 countries. It has yet to be cleared by the Russian government, but the BDI said further talks were planned in January to finalise terms and set a timetable.
Under the agreement, Russia would pay 25 percent of interest accrued since the start of 1992, while outstanding interest would be capitalised into the bonds.
Principal repayments would be suspended until they resumed in 2002 and would be completed by 2020, the BDI said.

The interest rate on the promissory notes will be fixed at 5.6 percent on dollar-denominated paper for five year, while mark notes will yield 4.6 percent. Rates will float thereafter 0.8125 percent over the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR).
The BDI, the Eastern Committee of the German Economy, and the Hermes export credit agency will ask 500 German creditor firms to register for the restructuring, the BDI said.
Following the London deal, the BDI said that prices for unpaid trade debts were likely to rise from their current 50 percent of face value.
"But a precondition is that political developments remain disruption-free in Russia," the BDI said, adding that the talks have helped boost debt's prices from 20 percent of face value a year ago.
